approved: Treasury Laws Amendment (Working Holiday Maker Employer Register) Bill 2017

The majority voted to agree with [the bill's](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fbillhome%2Fr5816%22) main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means that they can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? The bill was introduced to tighten the information disclosure requirements for the working holiday maker employer register. Firstly, it will ensure that details of the working holiday maker employer register will not be able to be made publicly available. Secondly, it'll ensure that information sharing between the Australian Tax Office (ATO) and the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) is only undertaken in situations in which an entity is non-compliant, or is reasonably suspected of non-compliance, with a tax law. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd088).

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-19.4.2) to agree with the bill's main idea. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). This means the Senate can now discuss the bill in more detail. ### What is the bill's main idea? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd088): > *The purpose of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Working Holiday Maker Employer Register) Bill 2017 (the Bill) is to make two amendments to tighten the information disclosure requirements for the working holiday maker employer register.* > *The first of the amendments is to the A New Tax System (Australian Business Number) Act 1999 (ABN Act) to ensure that details of the working holiday maker employer register will not be able to be made publicly available.* > *The second amendment is to the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (TA Act) to ensure that information sharing between the Australian Tax Office (ATO) and the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) is only undertaken in situations in which an entity is non-compliant, or is reasonably suspected of non-compliance, with a tax law.*

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-09-19.22.1) to pass the bill in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill for a [third time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). Since the bill was already passed in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. ### What does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd088): > *The purpose of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Working Holiday Maker Employer Register) Bill 2017 (the Bill) is to make two amendments to tighten the information disclosure requirements for the working holiday maker employer register.* > *The first of the amendments is to the A New Tax System (Australian Business Number) Act 1999 (ABN Act) to ensure that details of the working holiday maker employer register will not be able to be made publicly available.* > *The second amendment is to the Taxation Administration Act 1953 (TA Act) to ensure that information sharing between the Australian Tax Office (ATO) and the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) is only undertaken in situations in which an entity is non-compliant, or is reasonably suspected of non-compliance, with a tax law.*

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Working Holiday Maker Employer Register) Bill 2017 removes the public register of employers of working holiday-makers, increasing the risk of exploitation, and announced that Labor will oppose the bill.

The speaker opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Working Holiday Maker Employer Register) Bill 2017, arguing it would remove protections for working holiday-makers by eliminating a public register that allowed visa holders to check employer legitimacy. He accused the Turnbull government of siding with exploitative businesses and cited concerns about unconscionable exploitation, underpayment, and overwork of these workers.

The member for Grey supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Working Holiday Maker Employer Register) Bill 2017, which establishes a register to prevent exploitation of backpackers and sets a 15% withholding tax for registered employers. He also criticised the Labor Party for moving left and noted that 70% of young people in his electorate would not relocate for work, despite 14% youth unemployment.

Labor opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Working Holiday Maker Employer Register) Bill 2017, arguing it removes a public register that protects working holiday-makers from exploitation. The speaker criticised the government's backpacker tax negotiations and cited specific cuts: $17 billion from education, $15 million from Moreton schools, $92 million from Griffith University, $270 million from TAFE, over $3 million from QEII Hospital, $2.2 billion from Medicare, $1.5 billion from Queensland's GST share, and $375 annually from pensioners' energy supplement.

Opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Working Holiday Maker Employer Register) Bill 2017, arguing it removes a public register that would protect backpackers from exploitation as part of a deal with Senator Leyonhjelm. Criticised the government's mishandling of the backpacker tax, which damaged Australia's reputation and reduced backpacker numbers, costing Darwin hostels an estimated $1 million in revenue in the first week of the dry season, with a projected $1-1.5 million downturn and potential $8 million loss for Mitchell Street businesses.

The speaker argued that the government’s deal with Senator Leyonhjelm to remove the tax commissioner’s power to publish the working holiday-maker employer register would worsen exploitation, contrasting with the Treasurer’s earlier promise of public ABN Lookup transparency. Labor will work with the crossbench to defeat the bill.

The bill removes public access to the register of employers of working holiday-makers via ABN Lookup while maintaining registration with the ATO, allows employers to withhold tax at 15% up to $37,000, and restores ATO–Fair Work Ombudsman information-sharing to pre-2016 levels limited to suspected noncompliance.
